pairs.rationale: Different org kinds (eval-platform startup with customer/vendor/procurement stakes vs. robotics lab with a partner demo, course-plan search, and docs index) and genuinely different workload geometry — A is four identical 40×1-worker shard walls, while B mixes 40-slice runs with 10-point 3-worker sweeps and a ranked seed list that changes what 'partial' means. The rhyme is in the authorial tics rather than the story: each has a terse one-liner operator, a low-stakes yield-if-jammed persona, a manager-out-on-leave detail, an apologized-for wall of text, and a sick-kid aside, so voices feel written by the same hand even though the people and stakes wouldn't be confused.

The org skins differ (robotics demo lab vs. academic NLP group), but the workload skeleton and persona archetypes map almost one-to-one: a 40-shard/1-worker deadline owner facing a lock-in decision (Bianca/Petra), a 10-shard/3-worker ranked-priority search whose solo presenter has a manager/co-director absent (Rohan/Wendell), a terse one-liner operator (Bruno/Wes), and an explicitly deferrable low-stakes sweep (Elodie/Wes), all against the same 09:00 cutoff, same POLICY.md path, and near-identical token sizings. The main genuine divergence is Uma's stale-model-picker-board story and B's third 40-shard block, which shifts the demand mix slightly but not the underlying story shape.

The org shells differ — a robotics lab with four teams versus an eight-team applied-AI product org that adds genuinely new structure in the chained two-stage builds (Fernanda, Farid) — but A's roster maps almost one-to-one onto B's: the 40-shard cut-list gate (Bianca/Astrid), the ranked-seed search whose owner is up with a child's ear infection (Rohan/Jamal), the stale-index-or-board refresh that draws grumbling (Bruno/Jules), and the no-stakes sweep whose owner says bin mine first (Elodie/Felix). Verbatim persona tells recur — the ear infection, the manager on leave making the demo/lock 'mine', 'I never remember the numbers' about POLICY.md — so the voices and workload stories read as re-skinned rather than reimagined.

The org veneers differ (a robotics lab racing a partner demo vs. a consultancy assembling client acceptance evidence, 4 teams vs. 8), but underneath they share an identical substrate skeleton — the same 40×1-worker/~72M and 10×3-worker/~54M job templates, same 400k cap, same 09:00 cutoff, same 2x oversubscription, same POLICY.md — and the persona beats track closely: a terse stale-index/mistag complainer, a 'first two or three shards settle it' investigator, and a cheerfully cuttable low-priority tinkerer appear in both. Most damningly, Rohan's kid's ear infection is reused nearly verbatim as Carmen's toddler-ear-infection duty, which reads as a renamed persona rather than a new one.

The org kinds and stakes genuinely differ — a four-team robotics lab racing an overnight partner-demo run-of-show and mock-course route search versus a sixteen-team cloud ML platform juggling config freezes, gateway deploys, contracted labeling shifts and cold-storage migrations — and B adds gated two-stage 50-worker builds that A has no analogue for, with personas (Rohan's ear-infection deadline, Bianca's ten o'clock lock) that would never be mistaken for Sigrid or Signe. Still, A's four operators map fairly cleanly onto archetypes B also carries (ranked-priority sweep owner, terse 40-shard batch owner, self-deprecating low-stakes yielder) and both reuse the identical 40x1-worker/72M and 10x3-worker/54M job templates, so A reads largely as a small slice of B's archetype space in a new setting.

The org framings genuinely differ — a small four-team robotics lab racing a partner demo versus a sixteen-seat government evaluation consortium with charter filings, plenary windows and a new two-stage precedence archetype — and B's larger cast (Ilya's self-deprecating archival footnote, Gwen's reading-group slot, Ingrid's procedural charter claim) contains voices that would never be mistaken for A's. But the workload catalog is reused almost verbatim (40x1-worker ~72M batches, 10x3-worker ~54M sweeps with 'the early ones matter most'), and telltale persona details are recycled outright: Rohan's kid's ear infection reappears as Orla's toddler's, and Bianca's absent manager becomes Gaspard's manager on leave.

The worlds differ in org kind (a small robotics lab prepping a partner demo vs. a frontier lab's eight-team evidence/stakes ladder), scale, and workload mix — A's ranked seed search, run-of-show checkout blocks and decoding sweep have no counterpart in B's safety-verification/assurance/launch-qualification tiers and two-stage embedding builds — and the personas are unmistakably different in register, with A's operators carrying idiosyncratic personal stakes while B's speak in a deliberately uniform, stakes-declaring template. Residual rhyme is real but mostly substrate-level: identical cap, cutoff, policy path, an index rebuild in both, and the recurring 40×1-worker independent-slice shape.

realism.label: brb
realism.rationale: The voices have some genuine texture — Bruno's two-line brusqueness, Rohan's apologetic wall of text, the ear-infection detail, Bianca's absent manager — but every operator conveniently volunteers a clean internal priority ranking and two of them helpfully point at the same POLICY.md path, which is handoff behavior shaped by a grader rather than by colleagues. Economically the aggregate scale (105M budget, 400k output-TPM, 09:00 cutoff) is in the right range and the cap-vs-budget arithmetic doesn't contradict itself, but ~1.8M output tokens per single-worker checkout run, the absence of any stated worker pool size, and the too-tidy 72/54/72/54 = 252M totals undercut it. The 2.4x oversubscription plus one team explicitly offering to be dropped and two teams with diminishing-returns rankings is an unmistakable constructed-tradeoff frame.
realism.weakest_element: The job shapes are mirrored in exact pairs (Bianca and Bruno both 40 jobs / ~72M / 1 worker; Rohan and Elodie both 10 jobs / ~54M / 3 workers), which no real cluster night would produce.
